name: Paste
tagline: Store a local encrypted clipboard history with search, pinboards, and expiration

pricing.basis: annual billing, per user per month

tiers.name: Personal
tiers.limits: Use on all personal devices; no published device cap; includes updates.
tiers.notes: $29.99 billed yearly. Monthly and lifetime options exist, but their current numeric prices were not exposed in the crawlable public page.

tiers.name: Personal Lifetime
tiers.limits: Lifetime Personal access on all personal devices with updates.
tiers.notes: The live page offers this tier but did not expose its numeric checkout price.

tiers.name: Family
tiers.limits: Family-sharing plan sold through Apple's App Store; public numeric member cap and price were not exposed on Paste's page.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Team clipboard and administration plan; public numeric price and limits were not exposed in the crawlable page.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual + lifetime; 7-day trial on paid plans
pricing.hiddenCosts: Prices exclude tax and can vary by region. Family billing is App Store-only, and the current monthly, lifetime, and Team checkout amounts were not exposed in the public rendered page.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Paste, store a local encrypted clipboard history with search, pinboards, and expiration. The hard boundary is apple-platform polish, icloud sync, rich previews, and universal capture, plus os integration polish and maintenance.
coreLoopDIY: Store a local encrypted clipboard history with search, pinboards, and expiration in one focused macOS utility with keyboard-first controls and locally stored settings.
requirements: only the permissions required by the selected feature
whatYouLose: Apple-platform polish, iCloud sync, rich previews, and universal capture
commercial support and rapid compatibility fixes
ongoingBurden: permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Paste because small utilities are technically reproducible, but customers pay for polish and immediate fixes when an OS update breaks a daily habit. The recurring cost buys permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Espanso
priorArt.desc: Active open-source cross-platform text expansion utility with system integration.

alternatives.name: CopyQ
alternatives.desc: A clipboard filing cabinet with tabs, filters, rules, and built-in encryption.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Maccy
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Fast and local, but it lacks app-level encrypted history, pinboards, and expiration rules.

rejectedAlternatives.name: PasteBar
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Feature-complete and free for personal use, but its CC BY-NC license does not cover ordinary commercial use.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Paste plan and a single-purpose local Mac app DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Paste in an empty repository.
Use Swift 6, SwiftUI, AppKit where necessary, SQLite, and the macOS Keychain; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: store a local encrypted clipboard history with search, pinboards, and expiration in one focused macOS utility with keyboard-first controls and locally stored settings.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a menu-bar app with a searchable command window and global hotkey.
Implement only the primary feature and one settings screen instead of a plugin platform.
Request permissions just in time and explain why each is needed before opening System Settings.
Store configuration locally, support export or import, and never capture unrelated user content.
Add launch-at-login, update-check opt-in, diagnostics export, and a complete uninstall note.
Write unit tests for transformation logic and one UI test for the core keyboard workflow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a third-party extension marketplace.
Deliberately leave out cloud accounts and cross-device sync.
Deliberately leave out broad automation that executes untrusted scripts.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
